newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodians' dreams of peace, prosperity fade.
newsitem.headline: Cambodians' dreams of peace, prosperity fade.

text.p: Cambodians' fleeting hopes of peace and prosperity seem to have collapsed along with their coalition government after two days of fighting and a third of looting in the capital Phnom Penh.

As more of Cambodia's aid donors warned that their help might be halted in response to last weekend's ouster of Cambodia's First Prime Minister, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, ordinary Cambodians said it would be the poor who suffered from any cuts.
"It's not Hun Sen who will suffer, it's the ordinary people," said one young man referring to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen who ousted his rival Ranariddh.
"Hun Sen is rich already, he doesn't care about aid," said the man, who declined to be identified.
The United States announced on Thursday it was suspending its aid programme for Cambodia for 30 days.
Germany said on the same day it was suspending its aid programme and Australia said on Friday it was reviewing its assistance to Cambodia.
Foreign aid makes up half Cambodia's annual budget. Donor countries pledged $450 million to Cambodia at a meeting in Paris earlier this month. Last year, Cambodia received $500 million in aid.
The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) said on Thursday it was postponing Cambodia's admission to the group in response to the crisis. Cambodia had been due to join this month.

After decades of war, bloody revolution and international isolation many Cambodians saw membership of the dynamic grouping as confirmation that their country was finally on the road to prosperity as an equal partner with its neighbours.
But last weekend's street battles in Phnom Penh, which left 58 people dead and as many as 200 wounded, shattered many people's hopes for the future.
"I was very sad when I heard Cambodia was getting aid cut and would not be allowed into ASEAN," said student Chin Sophea.

"Cambodia will be alone in the region. We'll get poorer and poorer. Most people thought Cambodia was getting richer and would live in peace and stability, but now the exact opposite is happening," Chin Sophea told Reuters.
Others were nostalgic for the period of a United Nations peace process from 1991 to 1993 when large numbers of peacekeepers and election workers created a mini-boom in the impoverished country.
"I bought my taxi during the U.N. time," said driver Mea Bunthon. "But now there are no customers. If aid is cut people will live like they did in the 1980s again."
The Hanoi-backed government that ruled Cambodia during the 1980s was recognised by only a handful of countries, including Vietnam, the then Soviet Union and their allies.
But some Cambodians were defiant in the face of aid cuts.
"That's OK if America cuts aid. We lived all through the 1980s without American aid and we survived," said a civil servant. "I don't care about foreign aid, I only care about my family."
Others said international pressure would have no effect on Hun Sen.
"Hun Sen won't change his mind anyway. He does whatever he plans to do," said university student Som Buntha. "It's the ordinary people who live in misery, not Hun Sen and a few other rich people."
Other Cambodians said they did not care about foreign aid as they never saw any of it anyway.
"I don't know about foreign aid. I earn my money from selling fish," said market vendor Duong Konitha.
